buildUp: Start with the goal: a strong, steady and very even field over a region the size of a human torso. That points straight to a big solenoid, a tunnel of coils the patient lies inside.
Copper coils that strong would need megawatts of power, so the wire must be superconducting, and that means cooling it to about 4 K in liquid helium.

Liquid helium boils away if heat leaks in, so the coils sit inside nested layers: the helium vessel, a cold thermal shield, and an outer vacuum vessel, with a cold head on top to turn boiled-off helium back into liquid.
A simple solenoid's field is uneven and leaks out into the room, so the coils are split into several carefully spaced pairs, with reversed shielding coils outside and shims to iron out what's left.
To tell where signals come from, add gradient coils inside the magnet that tilt the field along each of three directions, switched in microseconds by powerful amplifiers.

Inside those goes the RF body coil to send the radio pulses, then a liner to make a smooth tunnel, a table to carry the patient to the centre, and receive coils close to the body to catch the faint echo.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Use the body's own hydrogen as millions of tiny radio transmitters. In a strong, even magnetic field, hydrogen nuclei can be tipped over by a radio pulse and then broadcast back at a frequency set exactly by the field they sit in. Make the field slightly different at every point and each spot in the body sings its own note, so a computer can untangle the chorus into a picture.

hardParts.title: A field even to a few parts per million
hardParts.why: To map position by frequency, the main field must be almost perfectly even, or the picture is warped and blurred. Getting a short magnet's field even to a few parts per million over a sphere half a metre across takes several coils placed to fractions of a millimetre, plus layers of shims to correct what is left.

hardParts.title: Keeping tonnes of wire at -269 °C next to a warm patient
hardParts.why: The superconducting coils sit only about half a metre from a patient at body temperature. Every watt of heat leaking in boils away helium, so the cryostat has to cut the heat flow to about a watt, using a vacuum, a radiation shield wrapped in many layers of film and supports that carry tonnes yet barely conduct heat.

hardParts.title: Switching huge gradients fast, quietly and safely
hardParts.why: Faster scans need stronger gradients switched more quickly, but each switch drives hundreds of amps through coils sitting in a field of several tesla, so they bang and vibrate. Switching too fast can even make a patient's nerves twitch, so the hardware is limited by human biology as well as by engineering.

principles.explanation: Every hydrogen nucleus in the body is a tiny spinning magnet that wobbles round the scanner's field at a frequency set by that field, and together they give a signal strong enough to measure. A hydrogen nucleus is a single proton, and it spins, which makes it a tiny magnet. In a strong field it wobbles round the field direction like a tilted spinning top, at a frequency proportional to the field: about 42.6 MHz per tesla, so roughly 64 MHz at 1.5 T. Only a few in every million more line up with the field than against it, but a body holds so many that their combined signal is enough to measure.
principles.title: Nuclei are tiny spinning magnets

principles.explanation: A radio pulse at the nuclei's own wobbling frequency tips them over, and how quickly they settle back afterwards depends on the tissue, which is what gives the picture its contrast. Like pushing a child on a swing, the pulse only tips the nuclei over if it matches that rhythm. Afterwards they keep wobbling together, sending out a weak radio signal, then gradually drift out of step and settle back. Fat, water, grey matter and tumours each settle at their own rate, which is why they look different.
principles.title: Resonance: push at the right rhythm

principles.explanation: If the field rises steadily across the body, the wobbling frequency rises with it, so each position has its own frequency. A gradient along the bore during the pulse picks out one slice; others during the echo give each point across the slice a different frequency and phase. A Fourier transform, the maths that splits a sound into its notes, turns the mixed signal back into a map of where it came from.
principles.title: Frequency tells you position

principles.explanation: A superconducting coil keeps its current flowing with no power supply and no heat, which is the only practical way to hold a field of several tesla over a whole body all day. Some materials lose all electrical resistance when cooled far enough. Niobium-titanium does so below about 9 K, so a current started in a loop of it keeps flowing for ever. Doing the same with ordinary wire, all day and every day, would need a power station's worth of electricity.
principles.title: Superconductors carry current for ever

firstPrinciples.problem: See inside a living body in fine detail, especially soft tissue like the brain, muscles and organs, without cutting it open and without the ionising radiation of X-rays. Soft tissues let X-rays through almost equally, so they look alike on an X-ray. You need a signal that comes from inside the body itself, that changes from one tissue to the next, and that you can trace back to the exact spot it came from.

questions.answer: The coils are made of superconducting wire, which only loses all its resistance when cooled to a few degrees above absolute zero, and liquid helium is the only practical liquid that cold. With no resistance, once the current is started it keeps flowing round the closed loop on its own, so the field stays on without a power supply.
questions.question: Why does an MRI scanner need liquid helium, and why doesn't the magnet need to stay plugged in?

questions.answer: The gradient coils. Each time a large current is switched through them inside the strong main field, the magnetic force makes the windings and the whole cylinder flex, like a loudspeaker cone. They switch thousands of times a scan, and different scans use different rhythms, which is why the noise keeps changing.
questions.question: What makes all the loud knocking and buzzing during a scan?

questions.answer: The superconducting magnet is always on. Its field pulls hard on anything containing iron, and the pull grows very quickly as the object gets closer to the bore, so a pair of scissors or an oxygen cylinder can be snatched out of someone's hands and fly into the magnet.
questions.question: Why are metal objects so dangerous near an MRI scanner, even when no scan is running?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The quiet genius of MRI is turning frequency into position. By deliberately making the field uneven in a precisely known way, with the gradients, the scanner gives every point in the body its own radio frequency, and the Fourier transform turns a single jumbled signal back into a detailed map. Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield shared a Nobel Prize in 2003 for this idea; everything else in the machine exists to make the field steady enough for it to work.

name: MRI Scanner
overview:
An MRI scanner takes pictures of the inside of the body without X-rays. Most of you is water and fat, and every hydrogen atom in them has a nucleus, a single proton, that behaves like a tiny spinning magnet. Put a person in a very strong, very even magnetic field and a few protons in every million line up with it. Give them a pulse of radio waves at exactly the right frequency and they tip over; as they settle back they send out a faint radio signal of their own, and how quickly they settle depends on the tissue they're in.

The scanner is built round that idea as a set of nested cylinders. On the outside is the main magnet: coils of superconducting wire, tens of kilometres of it, bathed in liquid helium at -269 °C inside a giant vacuum flask called the cryostat, so the current flows for years with no power. It makes a field of 1.5 or 3 tesla, tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's. Inside it, the gradient coils add small, carefully shaped changes to the field so that each point in the body sings at a slightly different frequency, which is how the scanner knows where each signal came from. Inside those is the radio-frequency body coil that sends the pulses.

The patient lies on a table that slides into the bore, often with a receive coil, such as a head coil, close to the part being scanned to catch the weak signal. The loud knocking and buzzing during a scan is the gradient coils being switched on and off thousands of times a second inside that strong field. A computer then turns the signals into slices through the body, sharp enough to show the brain's folds, a torn ligament or a tiny tumour.

parts.description: Smooth plastic shroud over the front half of the magnet, with the flared bore opening the patient slides into.

details.didYouKnow: Some children's hospitals cover their scanners in pictures of pirate ships or jungles and tell the story of an adventure, which can calm children enough that they need less sedation for a scan.
details.howItWorks: The cover is a smooth shell that hides the magnet, pipes and cables and gives the scanner its friendly, rounded look. Its front face curves into a wide flared opening, so the tunnel feels shorter and less enclosed to a nervous patient. It carries no load and plays no part in the imaging; it only has to be non-magnetic and easy to keep clean.
keyNumbers: Scanner about 2 m tall and wide
About 1.6 to 1.9 m long, front to back
Bore opening 60 or 70 cm across
details.madeOf: Moulded glass-fibre reinforced plastic or similar composites, painted white. No steel or iron is allowed anywhere near the bore, because the field would pull on it and distort the pictures.

parts.name: Front cover

parts.description: Matching shroud over the back half, which hides the magnet's pipes and cables and opens at the rear of the bore.

details.didYouKnow: The covers also carry soft sound-absorbing linings, because the inside of the scanner can be as loud as a rock concert while the gradients are working.
details.howItWorks: The rear cover closes in the back half of the magnet and the service end, where the helium pipes, power and cooling-water lines come in. The bore stays open at the back too, which lets air flow through and makes the tunnel feel less like a dead end. Engineers take it off to reach the cold head and the gradient connections.
keyNumbers: Bore open at both ends
Covers the cryostat's service end
Every fastener non-magnetic
details.madeOf: The same moulded composite as the front cover, fixed with non-magnetic brass or plastic fasteners.

parts.name: Rear cover

parts.description: Touch panel on the front of the scanner for moving the table, setting the laser marker and talking to the patient.

details.didYouKnow: The scanner room is a Faraday cage lined with copper, and even the window into the control room has a fine metal mesh in it, so that outside radio stations, phones and lights don't show up as stripes on the images.
details.howItWorks: The radiographer uses the panel to lower the table, position the patient and switch on a laser cross that marks the body part to be scanned. One press then drives the table smoothly so that mark lands exactly at the centre of the magnet. Most scanners have panels on both sides of the bore, and the scan itself is run from a computer in the next room.
keyNumbers: Usually one panel each side of the bore
Laser marker accurate to about a millimetre
Scan run from a separate control room
details.madeOf: A touchscreen or membrane keypad and small circuit boards, shielded so their electronics don't leak radio noise into the scanner's very sensitive receiver.

parts.name: Control panel

parts.description: Pedestal with motors that lift the table up to the bore and lower it so patients can climb on easily.

details.didYouKnow: Most hospitals also have a detachable non-magnetic trolley, so an emergency patient can be wheeled out of the room quickly without a metal bed ever going near the magnet.
details.howItWorks: Motors in the base raise the table to line up with the bore and lower it to a comfortable sitting height so patients can get on easily. It stands firmly on the floor just in front of the magnet. Everything inside is chosen to cope with being close to a very strong field, so there are no ordinary iron-cored motors near the bore.
keyNumbers: Lowers to roughly 50 cm for easy access
Carries patients up to about 200 to 250 kg
Lifts to the bore at about 90 cm
details.madeOf: A steel or aluminium frame with motors and gears inside a plastic cover; parts nearest the magnet use non-magnetic metals.

parts.name: Table base

parts.description: Long fixed beam on top of the base that guides the sliding tray all the way into the magnet.

details.didYouKnow: For whole-body scans the table moves the patient through the magnet in steps, scanning one section at a time, and the computer stitches them into one long head-to-toe image.
details.howItWorks: The table top is a long, stiff beam that holds the sliding tray level and guides it in a straight line into the bore. A belt or toothed drive under it moves the tray in and out to within about a millimetre. It must not sag with a heavy patient on the far end, deep inside the magnet.
keyNumbers: About 2 m long
Positions the patient to about a millimetre
Drives the tray at up to about 20 cm per second
details.madeOf: Aluminium and composite rails with a non-magnetic belt drive, under a plastic cover.

parts.name: Table top

parts.description: The cradle the patient lies on, driven smoothly into the bore so the part being scanned sits at the magnet's centre.

details.didYouKnow: Many trays have a spine coil built in under the mattress, an array of antennas that is always there, so back scans need no extra coil at all.
details.howItWorks: The patient lies on the tray, which slides along the table top until the part being scanned sits at the magnet's centre, where the field is most even. Receive coils plug into sockets built into the tray, so their signal cables travel with the patient. It is thin, so the patient lies as close to the middle of the bore as possible.
keyNumbers: About 50 cm wide
A few centimetres thick
Built-in coil sockets along its length
details.madeOf: Carbon fibre or glass-fibre composite: stiff, light and invisible to the scanner, with no metal to spoil the field or heat up in the radio waves.

parts.name: Sliding tray

parts.description: Soft, wipe-clean foam pad on the tray, so lying still for half an hour is bearable.

details.didYouKnow: Patients are checked for metal before every scan: some old implants, shrapnel and even certain tattoo inks can heat up or pull in the field, and a stray hairpin can fly into the bore at dangerous speed.
details.howItWorks: The mattress makes it possible to lie perfectly still for 20 to 45 minutes, which matters because any movement blurs the images. Foam pads and wedges are packed round the body part being scanned to steady it. The cover wipes clean and stops sweat or fluids reaching the tray.
keyNumbers: A few centimetres thick
Scans often last 20 to 45 minutes
No metal parts at all
details.madeOf: Foam inside a wipe-clean, waterproof vinyl or polyurethane-coated fabric cover, with no metal zips or springs.

parts.name: Mattress

parts.description: Flat array of receiving antennas built into the tray under the mattress, always ready for scans of the back.

details.didYouKnow: Each loop has to be switched off electronically during the transmit pulse. If it stayed tuned, it would pick up the far stronger pulse and could heat up or be damaged.
details.howItWorks: The radio signal from the body is faint and fades quickly with distance, so the best receiving antennas sit as close to the tissue as possible. This coil lies in the tray right under the patient's back. It is an array of overlapping copper loops, each with its own low-noise amplifier, so the scanner can combine their signals and take several in parallel to shorten the scan.
keyNumbers: Often a couple of dozen elements or more
Built in to the tray
Each loop has its own receive channel
details.madeOf: Printed copper loops and small amplifiers sealed in a flat plastic housing, with no magnetic metal. Tuning capacitors make each loop resonate at the scanner's frequency.

parts.name: Spine coil

parts.description: Cage of receiving antennas that fits round the head, close to the brain, to catch its faint radio signal.

details.didYouKnow: Using many small coils in parallel lets the scanner leave out some of its measurements and fill the gaps in later, a trick called parallel imaging that can make scans two to four times faster.
details.howItWorks: The radio signal from the brain is incredibly faint, so it is best picked up by antennas sitting as close to the head as possible. The head coil is a cage of many small loop antennas, each listening to the part of the brain nearest to it. Combining all their signals gives much clearer images, and lets the scanner take shortcuts that make scans faster.
keyNumbers: Typically 16 to 64 separate channels
Only receives; the body coil does the sending
Signal from the body is often less than a millionth of a watt
details.madeOf: Copper loops on circuit boards with tiny low-noise amplifiers, inside a plastic housing, with an open front and a small mirror so the patient can see out.

parts.name: Head coil

parts.description: Smooth plastic tube lining the tunnel the patient lies in, flared at both ends, with lights and a fan for fresh air.

details.didYouKnow: Moving from a 60 cm to a 70 cm bore sounds small, but it makes room for larger patients and noticeably reduces claustrophobia, so wide-bore scanners became very popular from the mid-2000s.
details.howItWorks: The liner is the smooth tube the patient sees, covering the RF coil and gradient coil behind it. It has small lights and a gentle fan built in so the tunnel feels brighter and less stuffy. It also acts as a barrier, keeping the patient a set distance from the RF coil's copper, where the radio field is strongest.
keyNumbers: 60 cm across in standard scanners, 70 cm in wide-bore ones
About 1.6 to 1.9 m long
Flared at both ends
details.madeOf: Moulded glass-fibre composite or plastic, transparent to radio waves, with LED lighting and an air duct.

parts.name: Bore liner

parts.description: Sixteen copper legs round the bore that send out the radio pulses which tip the body's hydrogen nuclei over.

details.didYouKnow: Some of the radio energy warms the patient slightly, so the scanner continually works out how much heat each kilogram of tissue is absorbing and limits the pulses to keep it safe.
details.howItWorks: The body coil is a giant radio antenna that sends pulses at exactly the frequency the hydrogen nuclei spin at, about 64 MHz at 1.5 T. Currents flow up and down its legs with each leg slightly out of step with the next, which makes a rotating magnetic field across the bore that tips the nuclei over evenly. Because it looks like an old-fashioned birdcage, it is called a birdcage coil.
keyNumbers: Usually 16 or 32 legs
About 64 MHz at 1.5 T, 128 MHz at 3 T
Fed by an amplifier of roughly 15 to 35 kW peak
details.madeOf: Copper strips on a glass-fibre tube, joined into the end rings through dozens of small non-magnetic capacitors that tune it to the right frequency.

parts.name: RF body coil (birdcage)

parts.description: Copper rings at each end of the birdcage, joining the legs through capacitors that tune it to the scanner's radio frequency.

details.didYouKnow: Feeding the coil at two points to make a rotating field was a big step: only the half of an ordinary back-and-forth field that rotates the same way as the nuclei does any useful work.
details.howItWorks: The end rings join the tops and bottoms of all the legs into one circuit. Small capacitors spaced round them set the coil's resonant frequency, like the tuning dial on a radio, so the coil rings strongly at the Larmor frequency and hardly at all elsewhere. The coil is fed at two points a quarter-turn apart, which makes the field rotate and halves the power needed.
keyNumbers: One ring at each end of the coil
Dozens of tuning capacitors
Fed at two points 90° apart
details.madeOf: Copper strip on the coil's glass-fibre former, with non-magnetic ceramic capacitors soldered across gaps.

parts.name: Birdcage end rings

parts.description: Thin slitted copper sleeve between the body coil and the gradients, keeping the radio pulses from reaching the gradient windings.

details.didYouKnow: It's a clever trick of frequency: the same small capacitors stop a slow current and pass a fast one, so one layer can be solid to the radio pulses and almost invisible to the gradients.
details.howItWorks: The body coil's radio pulses shouldn't reach the gradient windings, which would soak up their energy and could feed electronic noise back into the very sensitive receiver. This thin copper layer reflects the radio waves back towards the patient. Its slits break up the larger eddy currents that the gradients' much slower switching would otherwise set up in it.
keyNumbers: Often only a few tens of micrometres thick
Sits just inside the gradient coil
Blocks radio frequencies of tens to over a hundred MHz
details.madeOf: Very thin copper foil on a glass-fibre sheet, with a pattern of slits bridged by small capacitors. These look like a short circuit to fast radio waves but an open circuit to the slow gradient pulses.

parts.name: RF shield

parts.description: Thick resin cylinder holding the three gradient windings, water cooling and the iron shim trays, all potted in one solid tube.

details.didYouKnow: The knocking during a scan comes from here: every pulse of current makes the windings push against the main field, so the whole cylinder flexes like the cone of a giant loudspeaker, often louder than 100 decibels.
details.howItWorks: This thick cylinder holds the three sets of gradient windings, each set in its own layer, with cooling-water pipes between them because they carry hundreds of amps. Outer shielding windings cancel the gradients' field outside the cylinder, so they don't set up eddy currents in the magnet's metal. Trays of small iron pieces, the passive shims, slot into pockets along its length to even out the main field.
keyNumbers: Weighs around a tonne
Gradients of roughly 40 to 80 mT per metre
Switches at up to about 200 mT per metre per millisecond
details.madeOf: Copper windings set in epoxy resin reinforced with glass fibre, with copper or plastic cooling pipes, all potted into one rigid tube.

parts.name: Gradient coil former

parts.description: Saddle-shaped windings on the sides that make the field a little stronger to one side of the patient than the other.

details.didYouKnow: Real gradient windings look like giant fingerprints, with swirls of copper worked out by computer to give the straightest possible slope of field, not the simple saddles drawn here.
details.howItWorks: The X coil adds a small field that rises steadily from one side of the patient to the other. With it switched on, nuclei on the left spin slightly slower than those on the right, so the frequency of each signal tells the computer where across the body it came from. Its saddle-shaped windings sit in pairs on the sides of the cylinder.
keyNumbers: Hundreds of amps when fully on
Driven by an amplifier of up to about 2,000 volts
Switched thousands of times in one scan
details.madeOf: Copper conductor cut or wound into fingerprint-like patterns, bonded in the epoxy cylinder.

parts.name: X gradient coil

parts.description: The same saddle windings turned a quarter-turn, on the top, to grade the field from back to front of the body.

details.didYouKnow: MRI can cut slices at any angle through the body, which CT scanners of the 1980s could not, and that freedom is a big reason MRI took over for brain and joint imaging.
details.howItWorks: The Y coil is the same design as the X coil turned a quarter-turn, so it grades the field from the patient's back to their front. Using X and Y together, the scanner can tilt the slope in any direction across the bore. That is how it can take slices at any angle without moving the patient.
keyNumbers: Same strength as the X coil
Windings sit on top and bottom
Turned 90° from the X coil
details.madeOf: Copper windings like the X coil's, in their own layer of the epoxy cylinder.

parts.name: Y gradient coil

parts.description: Pair of loops carrying opposite currents that grade the field along the bore, from head to toe.

details.didYouKnow: The simplest version, two loops with opposite currents, is called a Maxwell pair, after James Clerk Maxwell, who worked out the arrangement in the 1870s, a century before MRI existed.
details.howItWorks: The Z coil grades the field along the bore, from head to toe, using loops that carry current in opposite directions, so the field is pushed up at one end and down at the other. Switched on during the radio pulse, it means only one thin slice of the body is at the right frequency to respond. That is how the scanner picks a single slice to image.
keyNumbers: Selects slices down to about 1 mm thick
Current reversed in each half
Strength similar to the X and Y coils
details.madeOf: Copper windings wrapped round the cylinder, in their own layer of the epoxy former.

parts.name: Z gradient coil

parts.description: Two of the six main superconducting coils, nearest the middle, where the field must be most even.

details.didYouKnow: A 1.5 T field is roughly 30,000 times the strength of the Earth's magnetic field, and it never switches off: the magnet is on day and night, even when nobody is being scanned.
details.howItWorks: Together the six main coils make the steady field that lines up the body's hydrogen nuclei. Current flows round and round them with no resistance at all, so once the magnet is ramped up, its supply is unplugged and the field stays on for years. The centre pair sits where the field has to be most even, over a sphere about 50 cm across.
keyNumbers: 1.5 or 3 tesla at the centre
A few hundred amps, with no power supply
Must stay below about -264 °C to superconduct
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconducting filaments, far thinner than a hair, inside a copper wire, wound tightly and set in epoxy on a precisely machined former.

parts.name: Main coils, centre pair

parts.description: The next pair out; with the others they turn a lumpy coil field into an almost perfectly even one at the centre.

details.didYouKnow: If a single turn of wire slips by a fraction of a millimetre, the friction warms it enough to start a quench, so magnet makers 'train' coils by ramping them up repeatedly before they leave the factory.
details.howItWorks: A single coil makes a field that is strongest in its plane and fades away either side. Using several coils of different sizes and positions lets their unevenness cancel, so at the centre the field varies by only a few parts in a million. The middle pair is spaced and sized to cancel the errors left by the others.
keyNumbers: Field even to a few parts per million at the centre
Tens of kilometres of wire in the whole magnet
Every turn placed to a fraction of a millimetre
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium in copper, like the other main coils, held rigidly so the huge magnetic forces can't shift the wire even slightly.

parts.name: Main coils, middle pair

parts.description: The largest main coils at each end, carrying the most turns to keep the field strong right out to the ends.

details.didYouKnow: The magnetic forces between the coils are enormous, many tonnes, pulling the end coils towards the middle; the coil former has to hold them apart with no visible movement at all.
details.howItWorks: The end coils carry the most turns because a short magnet's field droops towards its ends, and they make up for it. With the inner coils they make the field strong and even over the middle of a tunnel only about 1.6 m long. Earlier, longer magnets could use simpler coils, but patients disliked them.
keyNumbers: The whole magnet weighs roughly 4 to 6 tonnes at 1.5 T
Stores several megajoules of energy
Magnet about 1.6 m long
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconductor in copper, wound on a former and held against magnetic forces of many tonnes.

parts.name: Main coils, end pair

parts.description: Wider coils run backwards round the outside that cancel most of the field outside the scanner, keeping it safe nearby.

details.didYouKnow: Before active shielding, scanners needed hundreds of tonnes of steel built into the walls of the room to contain their stray field.
details.howItWorks: The shielding coils are larger loops near the ends that carry current the opposite way round. Outside the scanner their field cancels most of the main coils' field, so the stray field drops away within a few metres instead of filling the building. Inside the bore they cost only a little of the main field.
keyNumbers: Carry current the opposite way round
Shrink the 0.5 mT safety line to a few metres away
Usually two, one near each end
details.madeOf: Niobium-titanium superconductor, in the same helium bath and on the same circuit as the main coils.

parts.name: Shielding coils

parts.description: Thin layer of extra superconducting windings under the main coils that iron out the field's remaining unevenness.

details.didYouKnow: Shimming the magnet at installation can involve placing hundreds of small iron pieces in trays one by one, then measuring the field again, until it is even enough.
details.howItWorks: No magnet is built perfectly, and the steel in the building nearby bends the field too. The shim coils add small corrections, each shaped to cancel one particular kind of unevenness. They are set once when the scanner is installed, then smaller warm shims in the gradient coil are tuned for each patient, whose own body slightly disturbs the field.
keyNumbers: Correct the field to about one part in a million
Many separate shim channels
Tuned for every patient in seconds
details.madeOf: Thin layers of superconducting niobium-titanium windings on the coil former, plus room-temperature copper shims and trays of small iron pieces in the gradient coil.

parts.name: Superconducting shim coils

parts.description: Machined aluminium cylinder with raised ribs that locate each main coil exactly and hold it against the huge magnetic forces.

details.didYouKnow: A movement of a few micrometres in a coil can release enough frictional heat to warm the wire above its critical temperature and set off a quench, so windings are potted solid in resin.
details.howItWorks: When the magnet is at field, the coils pull on each other and try to burst outward with very large forces. The former locates each winding to a precision of a fraction of a millimetre, because a coil in slightly the wrong place would spoil the field's evenness, and it stops them moving. Even a tiny slip would release enough heat to risk a quench.
keyNumbers: Coil positions held to a fraction of a millimetre
Works at about -269 °C
Carries forces of many tonnes
details.madeOf: Machined aluminium or glass-fibre composite, or in some designs resin-bonded coils joined by spacers. Materials are chosen so they shrink with the windings as the magnet cools.

parts.name: Coil former

parts.description: A short length of superconductor with a heater on it, which closes the coils' circuit so the current can run for years with no power.

details.didYouKnow: This is why an MRI magnet is always on, even with the power to the building off. Taking the field away means deliberately ramping it down or quenching it, which is why metal objects are dangerous in an empty scanner room.
details.howItWorks: A superconducting loop needs a way to get current in. This short section can be warmed by a small heater so it stops superconducting. While it is warm, current from an outside supply is pushed through the coils. Then the heater goes off, the section cools and superconducts again, and the current flows round the closed loop with no power at all, so the supply can be taken away.
keyNumbers: Works in liquid helium at about -269 °C
Heater uses only a little power
Field can fade by only parts per million a year or less
details.madeOf: A length of superconducting wire wound in a compact, non-inductive pattern with a heater, held in a resin block. It sits in the helium with the coils.

parts.name: Persistent switch

parts.description: Sealed stainless-steel tank round the coils, filled with liquid helium at -269 °C so the wire superconducts.

details.didYouKnow: Helium is a non-renewable resource, recovered from natural gas, and one full magnet can hold more than a thousand litres, which is why scanner makers are racing to build magnets that need far less.
details.howItWorks: The coils sit in a sealed stainless-steel tank full of liquid helium, which boils at -269 °C, just 4 degrees above absolute zero. Nothing else is cold enough to keep the wire superconducting. Any heat that leaks in boils a little helium, which the cold head turns straight back into liquid.
keyNumbers: Traditionally holds about 1,500 litres of liquid helium
-269 °C (about 4 K)
Some newer magnets seal in just a few litres
details.madeOf: Welded stainless steel, which stays strong and doesn't turn brittle when deeply cold, with thin supports to hang it inside the vacuum.

parts.name: Liquid helium vessel

parts.description: Slim glass-fibre rods that hang the cold magnet inside the vacuum vessel while letting almost no heat travel along them.

details.didYouKnow: A scanner has to survive being trucked to the hospital, so the links have to cope with bumps from the road as well as just holding the magnet up, while still letting in barely any heat.
details.howItWorks: The cold magnet weighs tonnes, but anything that supports it also gives heat a path in from the warm outer vessel. Slim rods carry the load in tension, so they can be thin and long and still strong. Their small cross-section and low conductivity mean very little heat reaches the helium along them, and they also keep the magnet centred as it shrinks while cooling.
keyNumbers: Hold a cold mass of a few tonnes
Span from room temperature to about -269 °C
Only a handful of rods
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre or carbon-fibre composite bands or rods, which are strong but conduct heat poorly, with metal end fittings. They often connect to the thermal shield part-way along, so most of the leaking heat is intercepted at a warmer stage.

parts.name: Suspension links

parts.description: Aluminium shield wrapped in shiny insulation and cooled to about -230 °C, blocking heat radiating in towards the helium.

details.didYouKnow: Each layer of shiny film reflects most of the heat radiating onto it, so tens of layers stacked like the pages of a book cut the heat flowing in by many times.
details.howItWorks: Even in a vacuum, warm surfaces radiate heat, and the helium is so cold that a little of it matters. The thermal shield sits between the warm outer shell and the helium vessel and intercepts that heat, so the helium sees only a cold surface. The cold head's first stage keeps it at about -230 °C, so it soaks up heat cheaply before it reaches the helium.
keyNumbers: About 40 to 50 K (about -230 °C)
Dozens of layers of insulating film
Cooled by the cold head's first stage
details.madeOf: Aluminium cylinders that conduct heat well, wrapped in dozens of layers of shiny aluminised plastic film, called multilayer insulation.

parts.name: Thermal shield

parts.description: Outer steel shell of the cryostat, pumped to a hard vacuum so no air can carry heat in to the cold parts.

details.didYouKnow: The cryostat works on the same idea as a vacuum flask for tea, a gap with no air in it, but keeps its contents nearly 300 degrees below room temperature.
details.howItWorks: The vacuum vessel is the outside of the giant flask. Air is pumped out of it to a very high vacuum, so there is nothing to carry heat in by touch or by moving air, and only a tiny trickle of radiated heat is left. Its inner wall is the warm bore that the gradient coil fits into.
keyNumbers: Room temperature on the outside
Vacuum about a billionth of air pressure
About 2 m across
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or aluminium alloy, thick enough to hold the vacuum against air pressure pushing on it from outside.

parts.name: Vacuum vessel

parts.description: Steel feet that carry the magnet's several tonnes and spread the load over the floor.

details.didYouKnow: Installing a scanner often means cutting a hole in an outside wall or lifting the magnet by crane, because a full magnet is too big and heavy for hospital corridors and lifts.
details.howItWorks: The feet carry the magnet's weight and spread it over the floor. Scanners often sit on reinforced floors, and the room is planned so nothing iron like steel beams or lift shafts sits close enough to bend the field. Vibration pads under the feet stop the building shaking the magnet and the magnet shaking the building.
keyNumbers: Carry roughly 4 to 6 tonnes at 1.5 T
Heavier still for 3 T magnets
Usually set on vibration pads
details.madeOf: Steel or aluminium mounting feet bolted to the cryostat, with anti-vibration pads underneath.

parts.name: Magnet feet

parts.description: Two-stage refrigerator on top of the magnet that turns boiled-off helium back into liquid, so it hardly ever needs topping up.

details.didYouKnow: It takes thousands of watts of electricity to pump out just one watt of heat at 4 K, which is why every bit of insulation in the cryostat is worth having.
details.howItWorks: The cold head is a small refrigerator that pumps heat out of the magnet. Helium gas from a compressor expands inside it in two stages: the first cools the thermal shield to about 40 K, and the second reaches about 4 K, cold enough to turn boiled-off helium gas back into liquid. Its steady chirping sound, about once a second, is a sign the magnet is healthy.
keyNumbers: Second stage about 4 K (-269 °C)
Removes about 1 watt at 4 K
Compressor draws several kilowatts
details.madeOf: Stainless steel cylinders with a small motor and valve on top, and regenerators packed with materials that hold cold well, connected by hoses to a water-cooled compressor in a nearby room.

parts.name: Cold head (cryocooler)

parts.description: Neck rising out of the magnet where the cold head, helium fill line and current leads reach down to the cold mass.

details.didYouKnow: The current leads are normally plugged in only when the magnet is being ramped, then pulled out, because their copper would otherwise conduct far too much heat down into the helium.
details.howItWorks: The turret is the only route from the warm room to the cold mass. It holds the cold head, the helium fill and vent lines, the sensors and the port for the current leads that ramp the magnet. Every pipe and wire through it is a possible heat leak, so they are kept thin and long and tied to the thermal shield on the way down.
keyNumbers: Often the only opening in the cryostat
Crosses from room temperature to about -269 °C
Fitted with pressure-relief devices
details.madeOf: Stainless-steel neck tubes, chosen because stainless steel conducts heat poorly, with bolted and welded vacuum seals and pressure-relief fittings for safety.

parts.name: Service turret

parts.description: Flexible braided hoses carrying high-pressure helium gas between the cold head and its compressor in the equipment room.

details.didYouKnow: If the compressor stops, for example in a long power cut, the helium slowly starts boiling away. Hospitals treat a chilled-water or compressor failure as urgent, even though the magnet itself draws no power.
details.howItWorks: The cold head doesn't cool on its own: a compressor in another room sends it high-pressure helium gas, which expands inside the head to carry heat away, and the low-pressure gas returns along the other hose. The lines run all the time, and that rhythmic chirping you can hear in an idle scanner room is usually the cold head.
keyNumbers: Pair of hoses: supply and return
Gas pressure of around 20 bar
Compressor usually cooled by water
details.madeOf: Flexible stainless-steel hose with a braided outer layer and self-sealing couplings, so it can be disconnected without losing the gas. It is sealed and pressurised before delivery.

parts.name: Helium lines

parts.description: Wide pipe from the top of the magnet to the outside air, ready to vent the helium safely if the magnet ever warms up suddenly.

details.didYouKnow: Staff can quench a magnet on purpose with a big red button, for example if someone is pinned against it by a metal object, but it is a last resort: refilling the helium and ramping the magnet back up can take days and cost a lot.
details.howItWorks: If part of the wire stops superconducting, its resistance turns the magnet's stored energy into heat in seconds, boiling the helium. This is a quench. The pipe carries the rush of gas straight out of the building, because so much cold helium would push the oxygen out of the scanner room.
keyNumbers: Often 20 to 30 cm across
A litre of liquid helium makes roughly 750 litres of gas
A full quench can release over a million litres of gas
details.madeOf: Wide stainless-steel or aluminium pipe, insulated and sealed, running through the ceiling to a vent outside.

parts.name: Quench pipe

summary: A hospital MRI scanner: a superconducting magnet tens of thousands of times stronger than the Earth's field, kept at -269 °C in a vacuum flask round a tunnel, with gradient coils that tag each slice of the body and a radio coil that listens to the hydrogen in it.
